label: Harm from one more tonne of CO₂e

rows.label: Heat deaths caused by one more tonne of CO₂e (Rethink Priorities, GIVE model)

source.title: Clare & Vargas (2026), Cross-cause cost-effectiveness: climate change versus global health and development interventions, Rethink Priorities
source.page: Calculating the Mortality Cost of Carbon: Heat-Related Deaths, p. 16–17
source.quote: we estimate that the heat-related MCC is 4.31 × 10⁻⁵ (95% CI: 2.41 × 10⁻⁵ – 8.31 × 10⁻⁵)

rows.explainer: Deaths from higher temperatures, counted until 2300, caused by one extra tonne of CO₂ emitted in 2020: Rethink Priorities re-ran the GIVE model (Rennert et al. 2022, the model behind the US EPA's social cost of carbon) and counted the deaths themselves rather than their dollar value, so future deaths count in full, wherever they happen. The range is Rethink's 95% interval.

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths that come with one more tonne of CO₂e from fossil fuels (Rethink Priorities)

source.title: Clare & Vargas (2026), Cross-cause cost-effectiveness: climate change versus global health and development interventions, Rethink Priorities
source.page: Calculating the Mortality Cost of Carbon: Air Pollution Deaths, p. 17; Appendix C
source.quote: we estimate that the air-pollution MCC is 1.46 × 10⁻⁴ (95% CI: 2.48 × 10⁻⁵ – 4.28 × 10⁻⁴)

rows.explainer: Burning fossil fuels also releases fine particles, which kill far more people than the extra heat does. Rethink Priorities divides each paper's yearly deaths from fossil-fuel fine particles by that year's global emissions (Vohra et al. 2021: 2.93 per 10,000 tonnes; Lelieveld et al. 2023: 1.47; McDuffie et al. 2021: 0.30) and combines them with weights of 20%, 60% and 20%. It is an average: a tonne from coal carries more particles than a tonne from gas, and a tonne kept in a forest carries none.

rows.label: Deaths from heat and air pollution caused by one more tonne of CO₂e (Rethink Priorities)

source.title: Clare & Vargas (2026), Cross-cause cost-effectiveness: climate change versus global health and development interventions, Rethink Priorities
source.page: Appendix E (threshold BOTEC); Model 1 results, p. 18
source.quote: the median MCC estimate from our Model 1 Heat + Air Pollution (1.90E-04)

rows.explainer:
The default for the shared assumption "Deaths caused by one more tonne of CO₂": Rethink Priorities' median for heat and air-pollution deaths together, 1.9 per 10,000 tonnes. It matches Rethink's median cost per life saved of $10,517 at their median abatement cost of $2 a tonne (2 ÷ 10,517 = 1.9 per 10,000).

The low end, 0.43 per 10,000, is Rethink's heat-only scenario (no air-pollution deaths). The high end, 5.1 per 10,000, is the tops of Rethink's two 95% intervals added (heat 0.83, air pollution 4.28); it is also about what Rethink's whole-damages estimate, which adds crops, energy and sea-level rise (CG$1,600 a tonne at $100,000 per healthy year, 0.016 healthy years), comes to in lives at 32 healthy years each (5.0 per 10,000).

rows.label: Climate damage other than deaths, as a multiple of the heat deaths' value (not counted: 0)

source.title: Rennert et al. (2022), Comprehensive evidence implies a higher social cost of CO₂, Nature
source.note: Of the $185 social cost of carbon, about $90 is heat deaths; the other $95 (crops, energy, sea level) is 1.06 times the deaths' value. The high end of the range is that ratio; the best guess stays 0, our judgment.

rows.explainer: Said openly, like the meta charities' longtermist value: climate counts only the deaths a tonne causes. Lost crops, income, sea-level damage and tail risks are left at 0, a judgment, not a finding: no source turns them into healthy years on this site's scale. It multiplies the heat part of every tonne (1 + this), so changing it on a page moves every climate model alike. The range runs to the social cost of carbon's own ratio of other damage to death damage (1.06).

rows.label: Share of a won climate policy that is due to advocacy at all (all groups together)

source.title: Burstein & Linton (2002), The impact of political parties, interest groups, and social movement organizations on public policy, Social Forces 81(2), 381-408
source.note: Burstein & Linton review the studies published 1990-2000 in the main sociology and political-science journals: organisations influence policy in a minority of the cases studied, at most about half (the publisher's page shows a bot check; the finding as the abstract states it). Second reference class: Baumgartner, Berry, Hojnacki, Kimball & Leech (2009), Lobbying and Policy Change (University of Chicago Press), 98 randomly drawn issues lobbied in Washington: most saw no change over four years, and the side with more resources won only somewhat more often.

rows.explainer: When a climate rule, law or tax credit is won, how much of it was the advocates' doing, rather than what governments, industry, events and public opinion would have done anyway at the same time. Every advocacy group behind the win shares this (each model's attribution row gives the charity's part of all groups' resources), and the shared years a won reform counts say how long the win stands before it would have come anyway. From frequency to share: Burstein & Linton find organisations move policy in at most about half the cases studied, and Baumgartner et al. find that change usually doesn't come even when advocates push for it, and that resources predict it only weakly. If advocacy is decisive for about half of the wins it campaigned for and partly so for others, while the government's own agenda and events also had to line up, the advocates' expected share of a won policy is below one half. Our judgment, 30% (10% to 60%).

rows.label: Years from a won climate regulation or tax credit until its tonnes are avoided

source.title: US EPA (2023), Final rule for oil and natural gas operations: overview fact sheet
source.note: Anchors: EPA's oil and gas methane rule was signed in December 2023 and took effect in May 2024, with most existing-source compliance due from 2026-2027 (pushed to January 2027 in 2025); the EU Methane Regulation entered into force in August 2024 with leak detection from 2025-2026 and import limits from 2030; tax credits pay once plants are built, typically 2-5 years after the law.

rows.explainer: The wait from winning a regulation or a tax credit to the tonnes being avoided, discounted at the shared rate in each model. Our judgment, 3 years (1 to 6), from the compliance dates of recent rules and the build time of projects a credit pays for. A model whose policy states its own dates uses them instead.

rows.label: Years from work that speeds a new clean technology until its tonnes are avoided

source.title: US Department of Energy (2023), Pathways to Commercial Liftoff: Advanced Nuclear
source.note: DOE's pathway starts deployments around 2030 and ramps to about 13 GW a year by 2040 and 200 GW by 2050: the tonnes of a policy won in the mid-2020s come mostly in the late 2030s and 2040s.

rows.explainer: The wait from a policy or research win that speeds a technology not yet deployed at scale (advanced nuclear, new storage, novel fuels) until its tonnes are avoided: first plants, then the ramp. Our judgment, 15 years (8 to 25), anchored on DOE's advanced-nuclear pathway, where most deployment comes 15 to 25 years after today. Technologies further from market (fusion) wait longer: each model says so.

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths per tonne cut in US electricity, relative to the fossil-fuel average

source.title: Energy Innovation (2022) and Resources for the Future (2022), health modelling of the Inflation Reduction Act
source.note: Deaths avoided in 2030: about 3,700-3,900 (Energy Innovation), 700-1,300 (Resources for the Future), from roughly a billion tonnes cut that year.

rows.explainer: Per fuel and place, not the world average: US power plants mostly have scrubbers. Health modelling of the Inflation Reduction Act projects about 3,700-3,900 deaths avoided in 2030 (Energy Innovation, 2022) or 700-1,300 (Resources for the Future, 2022), from roughly a billion tonnes cut that year: 0.7 to 3.9 deaths per million tonnes, 0.005 to 0.027 of the world average of 1.46 per 10,000 (climate.deaths_per_tco2e_air_pollution). Best guess 0.013, the middle of the two studies' central figures on a log scale. Every model whose tonnes come from US power burning less coal and gas reads it in its fuel_smoke_factor.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂e a year the EU Methane Regulation's import standard would cut

source.title: Mendelevitch, Krieger & Loreck (2026), Assessing the GHG reduction potential of the EU Methane Regulation 2024/1787 on imports of oil and gas, Oeko-Institut Working Paper 3/2026
source.quote: Holding patterns and volumes constant, setting a methane intensity threshold in the range of 0.2% -0.4% can reduce GHG emissions by 95-120 MtCO2e.

rows.explainer: Methane from producing and shipping the oil and gas the EU imports came to about 155 million tonnes of CO₂e a year in 2023-2024 (GWP100 of 29.8, IPCC AR6); a methane-intensity limit of 0.2% to 0.4% on imports, which the regulation sets from 2030, would cut 95 to 120 million tonnes a year, holding trade patterns and volumes constant. Best guess 110 million, between the two thresholds (the limit's level is still to be set). The EU's own production rules (leak detection, venting and flaring bans, coal mines) come on top and aren't in this figure. How much of the cut is real rather than suppliers sending cleaner cargoes to Europe and the rest elsewhere is each model's counterfactual row.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂e EPA's 2023 oil and gas methane rule would avert, 2024-2038

source.title: US EPA (2023), Biden-Harris Administration finalizes standards to slash methane pollution (news release, 2 December 2023)
source.quote: 58 million tons of methane emissions from 2024 to 2038, the equivalent of 1.5 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide

rows.explainer: EPA's estimate for its December 2023 standards for new and existing oil and gas sources (40 CFR 60 subparts OOOOb and OOOOc): 58 million short tons of methane over 2024-2038, nearly 80% below what the sources would emit without the rule. EPA's '1.5 billion metric tons' of CO₂e is at an older warming potential (about 28.5); restated at the GWP100 of 29.8 (IPCC AR6) the shared climate conversion uses, 58 million × 0.90718 × 29.8 = 1.568 billion tonnes of CO₂e, about 105 million a year. Since 2025 EPA has extended its deadlines and loosened parts of it; the delivered share (climate.us_oil_gas_methane_rule_delivered_share) says how much survives.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂ EPA's 2024 power-plant carbon standards would avert, 2028-2047

source.title: US EPA (2024), Carbon pollution standards: fact sheet on the standards and regulatory impact analysis
source.quote: The RIA projects 1.38 billion metric tons total of CO2 avoided from 2028-2047 systemwide

rows.explainer: EPA's regulatory impact analysis for its April 2024 standards for existing coal-fired and new gas-fired power plants: 1.38 billion tonnes of CO₂ over the 20 years 2028-2047, about 69 million a year. EPA repealed most of the rule (the existing-source guidelines and the carbon-capture standards) in September 2026, effective 16 November 2026, and proposed repealing the rest; each model's implementation row says how much survives.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂ a year captured and stored because of the Inflation Reduction Act's larger carbon-capture credit (45Q)

source.title: MIT Technology Review (2022), Why the carbon capture subsidies in the climate bill are good news for emissions (Princeton REPEAT Project's estimate)
source.quote: US facilities would trap and sequester some 200 million metric tons of carbon dioxide per year
source.note: The article goes on: 'a 13-fold increase over what would likely occur with just the infrastructure bill that passed last year', which already held the 2018 credit. So about 185 million of the 200 million tonnes a year in 2030 are the 2022 law's doing. Delivery so far: CSIS (28 July 2025, https://www.csis.org/analysis/united-states-risks-losing-its-carbon-capture-advantage) puts US installed capture at 'over 20 million metric tons per year', about what was running before the 2022 law (some 22 million tonnes a year at 19 plants, Carbon Capture Coalition, 2024), against 'announced facilities under development with a combined capture capacity of over 130 Mtpa'.

rows.explainer: The 2022 law raised the 45Q credit (to $85 a tonne stored, $180 for direct air capture) and lowered the size a plant must be; the 2025 budget law kept it. Princeton's REPEAT Project projected about 200 million tonnes a year captured and stored by 2030, 13 times what the earlier policy (the 2018 credit and the 2021 infrastructure law) would give: about 185 million tonnes a year due to the 2022 law. Our judgment, 60 million tonnes a year once built (20 to 185 million), a third of the projection: the projection assumed pipelines and storage permits built at the pace needed, and by mid-2025 US capture running was still about 20 million tonnes a year, about the level before the law, with over 130 million announced but not built (CSIS, 2025). The high end is REPEAT's own increment.

rows.label: Ozone deaths caused by one more tonne of CO₂e emitted as methane

source.title: US EPA (2023), Regulatory Impact Analysis for the final oil and natural gas standards (EPA-452/R-23-013), section 3.6, citing McDuffie et al. (2023); and UNEP and the Climate and Clean Air Coalition (2021), Global Methane Assessment
source.quote: $1,800 per ton of methane (95 percent confidence interval: $760–2,800)
source.note: Global Methane Assessment (https://www.unep.org/resources/report/global-methane-assessment-benefits-and-costs-mitigating-methane-emissions): cutting 180 million tonnes of methane a year prevents about 255,000 premature deaths a year from ozone.

rows.explainer: Methane is also the main fuel of ground-level ozone worldwide, which kills people with lung and heart disease within about a decade of the methane's release, wherever it was emitted. Low: McDuffie et al.'s respiratory ozone deaths, valued by EPA at $1,800 per ton of methane, at a US value of a statistical life of about $11 million: 1.6 deaths per 10,000 tonnes of methane, 0.05 per 10,000 tonnes of CO₂e at a warming potential of 29.8 (respiratory deaths only, and below the full count where incomes are lower). High: the Global Methane Assessment's 255,000 deaths a year from a 180-million-tonne cut, cardiovascular deaths included: 14 per 10,000 tonnes of methane, 0.48 per 10,000 tonnes of CO₂e. Best guess 0.16 per 10,000 tonnes of CO₂e, the middle of the two on a log scale. The climate conversion adds it per tonne of methane (each model's methane_share row × this), valued like other air-pollution deaths and discounted over the years the extra methane stays in the air (climate.methane_lifetime_years): at 4% a year it counts 0.68 of its undiscounted value. For comparison, the shared conversion's discounted heat deaths are about 0.04 per 10,000 tonnes.

rows.label: Years an extra tonne of methane stays in the air (perturbation lifetime)

source.title: IPCC (2021), Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis, Chapter 7 (Forster et al.), section 7.6.1.1 and Table 7.15
source.quote: slightly revised since AR5 to be 11.8 ± 1.8 years

rows.explainer: Methane emitted today is broken down in the air over about 12 years: the extra methane falls by about 8% a year. Ground-level ozone follows the methane in the air, so the ozone deaths of a tonne come over those years, and the climate conversion discounts them that way: at the discount rate r their present value is 1 ÷ (1 + ln(1 + r) × 11.8), 0.68 of the undiscounted count at 4%. The deaths are taken in the year of the exposure; a lag from exposure to death (a few years in EPA's cessation lags) would lower them a little more and isn't counted. The range is the IPCC's ±1.8 years.

rows.label: Years until the heat deaths from a tonne of CO₂e emitted as methane

source.title: IPCC (2013), Climate Change 2013: The Physical Science Basis, Chapter 8 Supplementary Material, section 8.SM.11 (impulse responses for emission metrics: Joos et al. 2013 for CO₂, a two-box temperature response)
source.note: Derivation (our run of these standard responses): CO₂ airborne fraction 0.2173 + 0.2240 e^(-t/394.4) + 0.2824 e^(-t/36.54) + 0.2763 e^(-t/4.304); temperature response 0.631/8.4 e^(-t/8.4) + 0.429/409.5 e^(-t/409.5) K per W m⁻²; methane decaying over its 11.8-year lifetime (climate.methane_lifetime_years), scaled to equal CO₂'s forcing over 100 years (GWP100); heat deaths taken proportional to the warming, counted to 2300 like Rethink Priorities'. At 4% a year the discount-weighted delay is 60 years for CO₂ (the site's climate_heat_death_delay) and 23 for methane; undiscounted, a methane CO₂e tonne's warming to 2300 is 0.51 of a CO₂ tonne's. With heat deaths per degree rising 1% a year to 2100: 70 and 27 years, 0.37. The IPCC page blocks automated reads here; the parameters are the published ones as widely reproduced.

rows.explainer: Methane's warming comes early: it peaks about a decade after the methane is released and is mostly gone after a few decades, while CO₂'s lasts for centuries. Like CO₂'s heat deaths ("Years until the heat deaths from a tonne of CO₂", 60), methane's are discounted as if they all came this many years after the tonne. Running the IPCC's standard responses of temperature to a pulse of each gas, with heat deaths following the warming, gives 60 years for CO₂ at a 4% discount rate, the same as the site's figure, and 23 for methane. Our judgment, 23 (18 to 30): 20 at a 6% rate, 27 if heat deaths per degree rise over the century, which pushes them later.

rows.label: Heat deaths of a tonne of CO₂e emitted as methane, relative to a tonne of CO₂ (undiscounted)

source.title: IPCC (2013), Climate Change 2013: The Physical Science Basis, Chapter 8 Supplementary Material, section 8.SM.11 (impulse responses for emission metrics: Joos et al. 2013 for CO₂, a two-box temperature response)
source.note: Derivation (our run of these standard responses): CO₂ airborne fraction 0.2173 + 0.2240 e^(-t/394.4) + 0.2824 e^(-t/36.54) + 0.2763 e^(-t/4.304); temperature response 0.631/8.4 e^(-t/8.4) + 0.429/409.5 e^(-t/409.5) K per W m⁻²; methane decaying over its 11.8-year lifetime (climate.methane_lifetime_years), scaled to equal CO₂'s forcing over 100 years (GWP100); heat deaths taken proportional to the warming, counted to 2300 like Rethink Priorities'. At 4% a year the discount-weighted delay is 60 years for CO₂ (the site's climate_heat_death_delay) and 23 for methane; undiscounted, a methane CO₂e tonne's warming to 2300 is 0.51 of a CO₂ tonne's. With heat deaths per degree rising 1% a year to 2100: 70 and 27 years, 0.37. The IPCC page blocks automated reads here; the parameters are the published ones as widely reproduced.

rows.explainer: Tonnes of methane are stated in CO₂-equivalents at the 100-year warming potential (GWP100), which makes a methane tonne warm as much as a CO₂ tonne over its first 100 years; CO₂ goes on warming for centuries after, and the heat deaths of a tonne of CO₂ are counted to 2300 (Rethink Priorities). The same run of the IPCC's standard responses gives a methane CO₂e tonne 0.51 of a CO₂ tonne's warming to 2300. Our judgment, 0.5 (0.3 to 0.8): 0.37 if heat deaths per degree rise over the century (methane's come when it is cooler), and EPA's 2023 social costs value methane at about 8.5 times CO₂ per tonne at a 2% rate, 0.29 of GWP100's 29.8; the high end allows for deaths after 2100 counting less. The climate conversion multiplies methane's share of a model's heat deaths by this and discounts them over climate.methane_heat_death_delay: at the defaults a methane tonne's heat deaths are worth 2.1 times a CO₂ tonne's.

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths per tonne cut at US coal plants, relative to the fossil-fuel average

source.title: US EPA (2024), Carbon pollution standards: fact sheet on the standards and regulatory impact analysis
source.note: EPA projects about 1,200 premature deaths avoided in 2035 from the standards' fine-particle and ozone cuts, against about 123 million tonnes of CO₂ cut that year: 9.8 deaths per million tonnes.

rows.explainer: Coal plants' tonnes carry more smoke than the US power average (us_power_smoke_factor, 0.013): EPA's analysis of its 2024 coal and gas standards gives about 1,200 deaths avoided in 2035 against 123 million tonnes cut, 9.8 per million tonnes, 0.067 of the world average of 146 per million (climate.deaths_per_tco2e_air_pollution). Range 0.03 to 0.12, our judgment around EPA’s one snapshot year: plants retiring early cut less smoke per tonne than plants fitting controls, and the unhealthiest plants more.

rows.label: Tropical primary forest lost worldwide in 2023

source.title: World Resources Institute, Global Forest Review: How much forest was lost in 2023?
source.quote: Total tropical primary forest loss in 2023 totaled 3.7 million hectares

rows.explainer: World Resources Institute's count from the University of Maryland's tree-cover-loss maps. 2023 is used as a typical year: WRI's 2024 figure (6.7 million hectares, 3.1 billion tonnes) is a fire-driven record (WRI calls 2023 typical, like 2019 and 2021). With tropical_primary_loss_emissions_2023, the CO₂ released per hectare of tropical forest lost (about 650 tonnes), for every forest model; also the denominator of the forest branches' pandemic-risk rows.

source.title: World Resources Institute, Global Forest Review: How much forest was lost in 2023?
source.quote: All this forest loss produced 2.4 gigatonnes (Gt) of carbon dioxide emissions in 2023

rows.explainer: Gross emissions from the year's tropical primary forest loss (WRI). Over tropical_primary_loss_2023_ha it gives the tropics' average CO₂ per hectare lost, which every forest model uses unless a site's own carbon is measured.

rows.label: Hectares in an acre

source.title: US National Institute of Standards and Technology, Handbook 44, Appendix C (units of area)

rows.explainer: The international acre (4,046.856 square metres) in hectares, for every model whose source reports land in acres.

rows.label: Years from the EU Methane Regulation (2024) until its import tonnes are avoided

source.title: charityevals' judgment, shared by every model that counts this win (Clean Air Task Force, Environmental Defense Fund)
source.note: Moved from Clean Air Task Force's model (14 November 2026) so that every model counting the win reads one figure; value unchanged.

rows.explainer: The regulation entered into force in August 2024; importers report from 2025 and the methane-intensity limit was to apply from August 2030. The Commission proposed in October 2026 (COM(2026) 569) to move it to August 2031; the Council backs one year's delay, the European Parliament three. Our judgment, 7 years from 2024 (6 to 10).

rows.label: EU Methane Regulation: share of the import standard's tonnes that wouldn't have happened anyway

source.title: charityevals' judgment, shared by every model that counts this win (Clean Air Task Force, Environmental Defense Fund)
source.note: Moved from Clean Air Task Force's model (14 November 2026) so that every model counting the win reads one figure; value unchanged.

rows.explainer: Share of the import cut that is real abatement, not trade reshuffled or counted elsewhere. Oeko-Institut holds trade constant, but exporters can send their cleanest, certified cargoes to Europe and the rest elsewhere: comparing with Rystad's trade-adjusted figures it finds a diversion potential of about a third of import methane (p. 29), and argues that spillovers to producers' practice limit the leakage (p. 32), so about 54% of the 110 Mt is real. US gas is about an eighth of the cut (p. 4) and the EPA rule's delivered share of it (80% × 40%) is already in the US methane branch: −4%. 54% × 0.96 = 52%. Our judgment, half (20% to 85%).

source.title: charityevals' judgment, shared by every model that counts this win (Clean Air Task Force, Environmental Defense Fund)

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂ EPA's 2024 light- and medium-duty vehicle standards would avert, 2027-2055

source.title: National Association of Clean Air Agencies (2024), Summary of EPA's final multi-pollutant emission standards for model years 2027 and later light-duty and medium-duty vehicles
source.note: EPA projects cumulative CO₂ reductions of 7.2 billion metric tons over the life of the programme, through 2055 (7.7 billion under the proposal); EPA's own release (20 March 2024, https://www.epa.gov/newsreleases/biden-harris-administration-finalizes-strongest-ever-pollution-standards-cars-position) says 'more than 7 billion tons'.

rows.explainer: EPA's estimate for its March 2024 standards for cars, light trucks and medium-duty vehicles, model years 2027-2032 and later: 7.2 billion tonnes of CO₂ over 2027-2055, about 250 million a year. EPA rescinded the 2009 endangerment finding and repealed every vehicle greenhouse-gas standard in February 2026 (effective 20 April 2026); states and groups have sued. Each model's implementation row says how much survives.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂e a year the Inflation Reduction Act (2022) was projected to cut by 2030

source.title: Jenkins et al. (2023), Climate progress and the 117th Congress: the impacts of the Inflation Reduction Act and Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, REPEAT Project (Princeton ZERO Lab)
source.note: Our reading, not a quoted figure: REPEAT projected US emissions about 42% below 2005 in 2030 with the law against about 27% under policy then in force: some 15 points of 2005's 6.6 billion tonnes, about 1 billion tonnes a year; Energy Innovation and Rhodium Group projected somewhat less (Rhodium: 31-44% below 2005). The range spans the three groups.

rows.explainer: The whole law's projected cut in 2030 against the policies in force before it: clean-power, vehicle, efficiency, carbon-capture and methane provisions together. Best guess 900 million tonnes a year (600 million to 1.1 billion), the middle of REPEAT's, Energy Innovation's and Rhodium Group's projections. The 2025 budget law cut much of it back; each model's delivered share says how much survives, and a model counting only part of the law (the carbon-capture credit, climate.ira_45q_capture_tco2_per_year) subtracts that part.
